title: Patience

cards: A farmer has done everything a farmer can do. The field is plowed, the seed is in, the fence is mended. Now there's nothing left but the sky.
He can't make it rain. He can't pull the shoots up to hurry them. He can only stand at the edge of the field in the evening and wait.
The letter of James holds up that farmer as a picture, and yesterday Paul ended his riddle about hope with the same quiet word: we wait for it with patience.

teach.b: Here's James, in the King James words: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain."
Precious fruit. The farmer isn't bored. He's waiting for something he loves.
In the Bible, patience isn't only putting up with things. It's a kind of love.
Paul's chapter on love starts its list right here: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind." Charity is the King James word for love, and the first thing it says love does is suffer long. Love waits.

Then the Bible turns the same word toward God. When God passes before Moses on the mountain, he names himself: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth."
Longsuffering is part of God's own name in that passage.

And a letter of Peter answers people asking why the Lord's promised coming seems slow, in surprisingly tender words: "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish."

If God seems slow, Peter says, it's because God is waiting for people. So patience here isn't a gritted jaw. It's the farmer at the fence, the parent at the door at midnight, the friend who lets you take your time.
For Christians it's also the way God waits for them. Being patient with someone, in this picture, means loving them at their speed.

how: Christians count patience, called longsuffering in the King James Bible, among the fruit of the Spirit; churches teach it as something grown over a lifetime of prayer and practice.

o: gritting your teeth until a hard time is finally over
love that waits, like a farmer waiting for precious fruit
staying quiet so nobody can see that you're annoyed

s: in the Bible, patience is just putting up with things
Paul makes it the first thing love does: charity suffereth long.
"longsuffering" is part of how God names himself to Moses
"merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth."
Peter says God is slow because he has forgotten his promise
God is not slack; he is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish.

games.q: you're the farmer in James. the seed is in, and the rain hasn't come. what do you do?
o: pull up the shoots to see if they're growing.
wait with long patience for the early and latter rain.
games.why: the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it. he waits because the fruit is precious to him.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for right now, a person to change, an answer, a healing, a slow project, and notice where your body holds the waiting: a tight jaw, a restless hand.

Breathe into that place, let it loosen a little, and ask what it would look like to wait for this the way the farmer waits, for something precious. If you pray, you can bring it to God in James's words, be patient therefore.

wordCard.voice: Patience. In the Bible, longsuffering: the farmer's wait for precious fruit, the first thing love does, and the way God himself waits.

orig.note: Greek: patience, longsuffering — the word family behind "suffereth long" in 1 Corinthians 13:4.

carryVoice: Your line: love waits. Charity, the old word says, suffereth long. Rest well.
